_doc: Curated articles on the history of graphic adventures, written from web sources (see each 'sources'). English text; 'keywords' help searches in other languages. Where sources disagree, the text says so. Indexed by server/knowledge.py for Murray.

articles.title: Origins: from Colossal Cave Adventure to Zork
articles.keywords: origen orígenes inicio primera aventura conversacional texto historia Crowther Woods Zork MIT Ursprung Textadventure origine
articles.text: The genre starts with Colossal Cave Adventure, written by Will Crowther for the PDP-10 mainframe around 1975–76 and greatly expanded in 1977 by Don Woods at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab; the program, usually just called Adventure, spread to mainframes across the United States. In 1977 Dave Lebling and Marc Blank, at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science, discovered it and went on to write Zork. The Zork team founded Infocom, which between 1980 and 1989 released 35 text adventures. Scott Adams' Adventureland brought the form to home computers.

articles.title: Mystery House (1980): the first graphical adventure
articles.keywords: primera aventura gráfica gráficos Sierra On-Line Roberta Ken Williams erste Grafik-Adventure premier jeu d'aventure graphique
articles.text: Mystery House, released by On-Line Systems on 5 May 1980, is generally credited as the first graphical adventure game. Roberta Williams designed, wrote and illustrated it; Ken Williams programmed it for the Apple II. It had about 70 simple line drawings and no colour or sound. Sold by mail order, it soon sold some ten thousand copies. On-Line Systems, founded by the Williamses in 1980, became Sierra On-Line in 1982, and Roberta Williams went on to create the King's Quest series (1984–1998).

articles.title: Sierra On-Line: rise and fall
articles.keywords: Sierra historia caída venta CUC Cendant Havas Vivendi Activision cierre Oakhurst Geschichte Niedergang histoire chute
articles.text: Sierra grew from On-Line Systems into one of the leading adventure publishers of the 1980s and 1990s with King's Quest, Space Quest, Police Quest, Leisure Suit Larry, Quest for Glory and Gabriel Knight. In 1996 it was sold to CUC International (announced in February, completed in July 1996) and Ken Williams stepped down as president. CUC merged into Cendant in 1997; after the CUC accounting scandal of 1998, Sierra was sold to Havas. Sources differ on the details, but the Williamses left and the Oakhurst studio was closed around 1999. Sierra became part of Vivendi Universal in 2000; when Vivendi Games merged with Activision in 2008 the Sierra label was shut down, and Activision revived the brand in 2014 for re-releases and independent games.

articles.title: Lucasfilm Games, Maniac Mansion and SCUMM
articles.keywords: LucasArts Lucasfilm SCUMM motor origen Maniac Mansion Ron Gilbert Gary Winnick Aric Wilmunder cinemática cutscene Entstehung
articles.text: Maniac Mansion was conceived in 1985, when Lucasfilm Games asked Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick for an original game. To avoid writing it directly in a general-purpose language, Gilbert created SCUMM, the Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion. Credit for the engine is shared in different ways by different sources: Wikipedia says Gilbert wrote the original with early help from Chip Morningstar and that Aric Wilmunder enhanced later versions, while Wilmunder's memoirs and Lucasfilm's own history describe Gilbert and Wilmunder as co-builders. SCUMM was reused for Zak McKracken (1988), Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989), Loom (1990) and The Secret of Monkey Island (1990), among many others. Gilbert is credited with coining the term 'cut-scene', which was also a SCUMM command. Lucasfilm Games later became LucasArts.

articles.title: Ron Gilbert's 'Why Adventure Games Suck' (1989)
articles.keywords: ensayo manifiesto reglas diseño callejón sin salida morir Monkey Island diseño Essay Regeln règles conception
articles.text: In 1989 Ron Gilbert wrote 'Why Adventure Games Suck', a manifesto of his design opinions. It attacked conventions that were normal at the time, above all dead ends: in Maniac Mansion, as in most adventures of the 1980s, misusing an item or doing things out of order could leave the game unwinnable without the player knowing. The Secret of Monkey Island (1990) was built on those ideas: the player cannot die or get stuck, which became a hallmark of LucasArts adventures.

articles.title: Myst and the CD-ROM era
articles.keywords: Myst ventas CD-ROM best seller más vendido Cyan Miller The 7th Guest Verkaufszahlen ventes
articles.text: Cyan was founded in 1987 by the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller in their parents' basement in Spokane, Washington. Myst began as Rand's idea for an interactive storybook built in HyperCard on the Macintosh, and Broderbund published it in September 1993. It sold more than six million copies and was the best-selling PC game until The Sims overtook it (sources say 2001 or 2002). It was not the first CD-ROM showcase — The 7th Guest had already shown what the medium could do — but it became the best-selling CD-ROM game of 1993 and helped push CD-ROM drives into homes.

articles.title: The decline of the late 1990s
articles.keywords: declive muerte del género fin crisis años 90 por qué murieron las aventuras gráficas shooters 3D Niedergang Tod des Genres déclin mort du genre
articles.text: By the late 1990s the classic adventure was in decline. Commentators point to several causes, none of them settled: the market grew faster for action and 3D genres such as shooters, publishers shifted budgets away from adventures, and by around 2000 very few adventures were in development. At Sierra, management changes after the 1996 sale left Ken and Roberta Williams less involved. At LucasArts, Grim Fandango (1998) won awards such as GameSpot's Game of the Year but sold modestly, and Escape from Monkey Island (2000) was its last original adventure. LucasArts' money came mainly from Star Wars games.

articles.title: The end of LucasArts
articles.keywords: LucasArts cierre Disney 2013 Double Fine Tim Schafer Schließung fermeture
articles.text: Tim Schafer left LucasArts shortly after Grim Fandango and founded Double Fine in 2000. LucasArts cancelled its adventure sequels in the early 2000s; the cancellation of Sam & Max: Freelance Police led former staff to found Telltale Games in 2004. After Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012, LucasArts' in-house development was closed in April 2013 and the name survived as a licensor of Lucasfilm properties.

articles.title: Telltale Games and episodic adventures
articles.keywords: Telltale episodios episódico The Walking Dead cierre 2018 Episoden épisodes
articles.text: Telltale Games was founded in 2004 by former LucasArts employees after the cancellation of Sam & Max: Freelance Police, to carry on LucasArts-style adventures. It tested the episodic format first with Jeff Smith's Bone comics, then made Sam & Max and Tales of Monkey Island seasons. From 2012, with The Walking Dead, it shifted to choice-driven story games and produced thirteen seasons between 2012 and 2018. On 21 September 2018 almost all staff were laid off without warning; the assets were sold off later that year, and in 2019 LCG Entertainment revived the Telltale name with many of its licences.

articles.title: The crowdfunding revival: Double Fine Adventure
articles.keywords: Kickstarter micromecenazgo crowdfunding renacimiento resurgir Broken Age Double Fine Thimbleweed Park Wiederbelebung renouveau financement participatif
articles.text: In February 2012 Double Fine launched 'Double Fine Adventure' on Kickstarter, asking for $400,000 to make a classic point-and-click adventure. It broke the platform's records for money raised in 24 hours and number of backers, and closed with about $3.3 million from more than 87,000 backers. The game became Broken Age (2014–2015). Its success showed publishers that an audience for the genre still existed and opened the door to other crowdfunded adventures, such as Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick's Thimbleweed Park (2017).

articles.title: ScummVM: keeping the classics playable
articles.keywords: ScummVM emulador preservación jugar hoy clásicos Strigeus Erhaltung préservation
articles.text: ScummVM was started in September 2001 by Ludvig Strigeus, a computer science student, with a first public release in October; Vincent Hamm, who had been writing his own SCUMM player, joined that year. It began with Monkey Island 2 and grew far beyond SCUMM: today it reimplements the engines of hundreds of adventures from Sierra, Revolution, Westwood, Coktel Vision and many others, as free software under the GNU GPL. Several companies have released old games as freeware through ScummVM.

articles.title: Adventure Game Studio and the indie scene
articles.keywords: AGS indie independientes Wadjet Eye Blackwell motor gratuito Chris Jones unabhängig indépendant
articles.text: Adventure Game Studio began in 1997 as an MS-DOS program called Adventure Creator, written by British programmer Chris Jones; rewritten, it was released as Adventure Game Studio in September 1999. Its free editor made it the backbone of the amateur and indie adventure scene for decades. Jones released the editor's source code under the Artistic License 2.0 in October 2010 and the runtime in 2011. Dave Gilbert incorporated Wadjet Eye Games in October 2006; its Blackwell series and many games it publishes, such as Gemini Rue, Primordia, Unavowed and The Excavation of Hob's Barrow, are made with AGS.

articles.title: Revolution Software
articles.keywords: Revolution Software Charles Cecil Broken Sword Beneath a Steel Sky británica York Hull
articles.text: Revolution Software was founded by Charles Cecil, Tony Warriner, David Sykes and Noirin Carmody (Wikipedia says 1989; other sources say March 1990), at first in Hull — reportedly above a fruit market — and from 1994 in York. Cecil became managing director and focused on writing and design. Its games include Lure of the Temptress (1992), Beneath a Steel Sky (1994, with art by Dave Gibbons) and the Broken Sword series from 1996.

articles.title: Spanish adventures: Aventuras AD and Pendulo Studios
articles.keywords: aventuras españolas España Aventuras AD Andrés Samudio Dinamic Pendulo Igor Hollywood Monsters Runaway Alcachofa Drascula conversacionales
articles.text: Spain had its own adventure tradition. Aventuras AD, split from Dinamic Software (sources give 1987 or 1988), specialised in text adventures — La Aventura Original, Jabato, La Diosa de Cozumel — with Andrés Samudio as its key figure, and closed around 1992. Pendulo Studios was founded in Madrid in 1993 or 1994 (sources differ) by Ramón Hernáez, Felipe Gómez Pinilla, Rafael Latiegui and Miguel Ángel Ramos; after Igor: Objetivo Uikokahonia, Hollywood Monsters was its turning point, followed by the Runaway series. Alcachofa Soft made Drascula: The Vampire Strikes Back (1996), later released as freeware.

articles.title: Interactive fiction after Infocom
articles.keywords: ficción interactiva aventura de texto Inform Graham Nelson Curses Magnetic Scrolls Level 9 The Pawn Photopia interaktive Fiktion fiction interactive
articles.text: Text adventures did not die with Infocom. In the UK, Level 9 and Magnetic Scrolls led the 1980s; Magnetic Scrolls' first game, The Pawn (1985), was known for a powerful parser and 16-colour pictures. In 1993 Graham Nelson created Inform, a language that compiled to Infocom's Z-machine format, and released Curses, which players greeted as 'almost like having Infocom back'. An online interactive fiction community grew around Usenet and yearly competitions; Adam Cadre's Photopia won the 1998 competition.

articles.title: Return to Monkey Island (2022)
articles.keywords: Return to Monkey Island regreso Gilbert Grossman Devolver 2022
articles.text: Return to Monkey Island is a point-and-click adventure developed by Terrible Toybox and published by Devolver Digital. Ron Gilbert directed it and wrote and designed it with Dave Grossman — the pair's return to the series 31 years after Monkey Island 2. It was released on 19 September 2022 for macOS, Nintendo Switch and Windows, and later on other platforms, to generally positive reviews.
